title: W5: Summarising Distributions II
text:
Pick someone new to be the driver this week. They will type the code. The rest of you are navigators, you need to tell the driver where to go (i.e., what to type!).
Driver instructions:

Log in to the bigger screen at your table
Open RStudio Server

Question 1


We’re continuing to use the same dataset for the next couple of weeks (the survey that many of you completed in the first week). The data are stored at https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv (Check back to your work from the previous weeks to remind yourself how to get the data into R).
Calculate the Inter Quartile Range (IQR) for:

distance_born - the distances from Edinburgh that the respondents were born. The IQR is appropriate here because the variable is highly skewed.

spicy_num - the levels of spice that respondents like. The IQR is appropriate here because the variable is ordinal.


🗂️ See Measure variability > IQR flash card.






Solution



Solution 1. 

library(tidyverse)
sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv")

sdata |> 
  summarise(
    dist_IQR = IQR(distance_born, na.rm = TRUE),
    spice_IQR = IQR(spicy_num, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  dist_IQR spice_IQR
     <dbl>     <dbl>
1    1569.       0.5






Question 2


The survey also asked people to rate, on scales of 0 to 100, three things:







variable
question




sleepqual
“how well do you tend to sleep on average?”


procrast
“how often do you tend to procrastinate on tasks or responsibilities on average?”


multitask
“how well do you think you can handle multiple tasks or responsibilities at the same time on average?”



Calculate the mean and standard deviation for one of these variables.

🗂️ See Measure variability > SD flash card.






Solution



Solution 2. 

sdata |> 
  summarise(
    sleep_M = mean(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE),
    sleep_SD = sd(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE),
    procr_M = mean(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    procr_SD = sd(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    mutli_M = mean(multitask, na.rm = TRUE),
    multi_SD = sd(multitask, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  sleep_M sleep_SD procr_M procr_SD mutli_M multi_SD
    <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
1      62     15.6      28     5.60      35     22.0






Question 3


For the sleep-quality, procrastination, and multitasking variables, respondents were given the scale from 0 to 100. That doesn’t necessarily mean that people used the whole scale.
For the same variable you chose in the previous question, calculate its range.

🗂️ See Measure variability > Range flash card.






Solution



Solution 3. 

sdata |> 
  summarise(
    sleep_R = max(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE) - min(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  sleep_R
    <dbl>
1      35






Question 4


In one call to summarise() (that is, using the function summarise() only once), calculate descriptive statistics of central tendency and variability for all three variables sleepqual, procrast and multitask.





Solution



Solution 4. 

sdata |> 
  summarise(
    sleep_m = mean(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE),
    sleep_s = sd(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE),
    procr_m = mean(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    procr_s = sd(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    multi_m = mean(multitask, na.rm = TRUE),
    multi_s = sd(multitask, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  sleep_m sleep_s procr_m procr_s multi_m multi_s
    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1      62    15.6      28    5.60      35    22.0

The survey also included questions asking about whether people perceive themselves as pessimists vs optimists (the outlook variable), and as an “evening person” vs a “morning person” (the ampm variable).

title: W1: Introductions
text:
This week’s workshop is quite minimal. All we’re really wanting you to do is:

Explore the software and start playing around.

Meet some new people, make some new friends, and form a group to work with in these workshops.

From next week, you’ll be working in these groups collaboratively on the workshop questions, with one person doing the typing (the ‘driver’) and the others telling them what to type (the ‘navigators’). The role of driver will swap each week, so you’ll always get a turn at typing.


Question 1


The very first task here is to open RStudio.
R and RStudio is software that you can download and install on your computer, but for the duration of this course, we are providing you with a version on a server.
You can access the RStudio server here: https://rstudio.ppls.ed.ac.uk.
We would recommend you bookmark the page so that you can easily find it again!




Question 2


The first thing to do is start using R just like a calculator.
Try doing some basic calculations by typing in the bottom left where you see the blue > and pressing enter.
Playing with these: *, /, +, -, ^ and seeing what happens - can you work out what each one does?






stuck seeing a + symbol?





If we give R an incomplete request, then it will just stay waiting for it to be finished.
e.g., if we typed a query and missed a bracket, then R would just leave a + symbol to say “I’m waiting for more…”:

To get out of this we can either type the required stuff to finish the query, or, much more simply, just press the Escape key (Esc) and it will cancel the query and let you start it again.







Question 3


In order to save our work, we need to start writing our commands in a document. Something we can edit, save, come back to later on, and share with other people.

Open an R Script (File > New File > R Script).

A new window will pop up in the top left of RStudio. Write some calculations in there (put each one on a new line).

You’ll notice that writing in the script doesn’t actually perform the calculations. We need to “Run” the commands we are writing, which we can do by ensuring the cursor is on the line we want to run, and then either:

press Ctrl+Enter (or Cmd+Enter for Mac)OR
clicking the “Run” button in the top right of the R Script.






Question 4



my_name <- "Umberto"
about_me <- "Italian."
fun_fact <- "I can play the piano."
# starting a line with a "#" turns it into a comment
# it means that R will not try to run it  

# this is a "function". it takes some inputs, and gives us outputs
# in this case, we give it a whole load of separate sentence fragments
# and it sticks them together: 
paste("Hello, my name is", my_name, 
      "and I am", about_me,
      "Fun fact:", fun_fact)


Copy-Paste the lines of code above into your R Script and edit them to provide some text about yourself (if you don’t want to share a fun fact about yourself, just share a random fun fact!)
Save your script (File > Save).
Close your script (there’s a little cross in the tab label at the top of the script)
Re-open your script (File > Open)
Celebrate!

Groups are named based on the workshop (1, 2, 3, 4) and your table number.
So if this is Workshop 3, and you are sitting at table 6, you should join group “WS3.6”.

Go to the course LEARN page
click Groups on the top menu bar.
click Workshops_1_2_3_4

Now click on “Group Discussion Space” in the top menu of the course LEARN page.
Upload your script to the discussion space, to share your fun fact with your group members.

Question 5


R will by default treat a variable with only numbers in it as a numeric variable, and anything else as a “character” variable (“character” = any letters/numbers/symbols).
Change the eye_colour variable to a factor in R, that only has the options “brown”, “blue”, “green” or “hazel”.

🗂️ See Mutate columns and Manage factor variables flash cards.

What happens when you now do skim(data)? How does it treat this variable differently?






Hints





Here is the basic code structure for taking a dataframe named mydata and adding a new variable (or changing an existing one).

Line 2 takes the data, and passes it to line 3.

Lines 3-5 “mutates” the data, adding a variable called new_variable. The new_variable is going to contain the values of an existing variable (old_variable) but with some function applied to them. For example, if we had new_variable = old_variable/2 then it would contain the same values but halved.
It feels odd, but it helps to think about the first line of code once we’ve thought of the others. This line re-assigns the name mydata to the mutated mydata, thereby making the change save to the object in R’s memory.


mydata <-
  mydata |> 
  mutate(
    new_variable = function(old_variable)
  )

To make a variable a factor, the function we want is factor(). This will consider every different value that we have to be a possible category:

factor(variable)

If we want to have a specific set of possible values, we can do so with the levels part of the function, replacing the "..." with the options we consider valid:

factor(variable, levels = c("...","...","...", ....... ))











Solution



Solution 5. 

sdata <-
  sdata |>
  mutate(
    eye_colour = factor(eye_colour, levels = c("brown","blue","green","hazel"))
  )

title: W4: Summarising Distributions I
text:
Pick someone new to be the driver this week. They will type the code. The rest of you are navigators, you need to tell the driver where to go (i.e., what to type!).
Driver instructions:

Log in to the bigger screen at your table
Open RStudio Server
Listen to your navigators

Navigator instructions:

Tell your driver where to go (i.e., what to type)!



Question 1


We’re continuing to use the same dataset for the next couple of weeks (the survey that many of you completed in the first week). The data are stored at https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv (Check back to your work from the previous two weeks to remind yourself how to get the data into R).
What was the most common month in which survey respondents were born?

🗂️ See Measure central tendency > Mode flash card.







Hint





The variable that holds this information is the one called birthmonth. You can check what different variables are in your data by quickly using names(data), replacing “data” with whatever name you used to store your dataset in R.








Solution



Solution 1. 

library(tidyverse)
sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv")

sdata |> 
  count(birthmonth)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  birthmonth     n
  <chr>      <int>
1 february       1
2 january        2
3 july           1






Question 2


One of the questions in the survey asked about how spicy people liked their food.
The possible responses were:


Anti-spice: Mayonnaise is too spicy for me; I avoid any black pepper.
Mild: I like a tiny hint of warmth, but flavour comes first.
Medium: I enjoy a solid kick that makes the meal interesting.
Hot: I want to feel the burn.
Very Hot: I want to sweat and question my life choices.
Extreme: I want to transcend mortal existence and taste the fury of a thousand suns.


This has been recoded for you already so that the dataset contains both a variable with the descriptive word (“medium”, “hot” etc), and a variable with a numeric value (1 being assigned to “anti-spice” and 6 being assigned to “extreme”).
For what level of spicy-ness does half of the sample fall above and half fall below?

🗂️ See Measure central tendency > Median flash card.






Solution



Solution 2. 

sdata |> 
  summarise(
    spicy_Med = median(spicy_num, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  spicy_Med
      <dbl>
1         3






Question 3


Another question asked respondents to rate the quality of their sleep (from 0 to 100). On average, how well did respondents sleep?
What was the average sleep quality rating

🗂️ See Measure central tendency > Mean flash card.






Solution



Solution 3. 

sdata |>
  summarise(
    sleep_M = mean(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  sleep_M
    <dbl>
1      62






Question 4


The code below creates a visualisation of the “distance-from-Edinburgh” that respondents were born (you may need to replace the sdata with whatever you named your dataset in R):

ggplot(sdata, aes(x = distance_born)) +
  geom_histogram()








Do you think the median or the mean of this variable will be higher?
Calculate both the mean and median for this variable to see if you were right. (Challenge: calculate both summary statistics within the same instance of summarise().)





Solution



Solution 4. 

sdata |>
  summarise(
    dist_M = mean(distance_born),
    dist_Med = median(distance_born)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2

text:

Question 1


We’re continuing to use the same survey data for the remainder of the semester. The data are stored at https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv. By now, as a group you will have read in the data numerous times. Just check back to your work from the previous weeks to remind yourself if needs be.
This week we are working with the two questions about peoples outlook (pessimism/optimism) and their chronotype (evening/morning person).

These are on quite different scales (-100 to 100, and 0 to 10). Which means someone scoring 10 on outlook means a very different thing to them scoring 10 on ampm.
Task: Read in the data, and create two new variables, which are the standardised (or Z-) scores on these variables.

TODO






Solution



Solution 1. 

library(tidyverse)
sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv")

sdata <- sdata |>
  mutate(
    outlookZ = ( outlook - mean(outlook) ) / sd(outlook),
    ampmZ = ( ampm - mean(ampm) ) / sd(ampm)
  )





Question 2


Find the pseudonyms, scores, and Z-scores of the three people who reported being the most optimistic, and the three who identified the most as “morning people”.






Hint





One way to do this is to take the data (line 1 below), and then sort it by a variable, in descending order (line 2), before taking a “slice” of it and asking for specific row numbers (line 3). You can then, to make it easier to see stuff in the output, choose only the variables that you want to see (line 4):

data |>
  arrange(desc(variable)) |>
  slice(1:5) |>
  select(variable, variable2, variable3)

TODO flash?








Solution



Solution 2. 

sdata |> 
  arrange(desc(outlook)) |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  select(pseudonym, outlook, outlookZ)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  pseudonym    outlook outlookZ
  <chr>          <dbl>    <dbl>
1 rufus             74    1.38 
2 allscratch        20    0.106
3 noodle_horse     -16   -0.741

sdata |> 
  arrange(desc(ampm)) |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  select(pseudonym, ampm, ampmZ)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  pseudonym     ampm   ampmZ
  <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 allscratch    10    1.18  
2 noodle_horse   9.4  0.131 
3 dougal         9.3 -0.0436






Question 3


Plot the standardised outlook scores as a density curve.
Once you have made your plot, add this bit of code to the end of it. It will add a normal distribution (with mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1).

... 
  ... +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), 
                colour = "red")


🗂️ See the Plot a variable > Histogram flash card. Only we don’t want a geom_histogram(), we want a geom_density()!






Solution



Solution 3. 

ggplot(sdata , aes(x = outlookZ)) +
  geom_density() +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), colour = "red")












Question 4

















Rabbit hole: how to find this out for any %





In “the olden days” when everything was black and white, there were big tables of numbers that people had to look through to figure out this sort of thing.
Computers can do it in an instant. The qnorm() function in R takes a probability, and returns the value at which that area under the normal distribution falls.
Computers can do this in an instant. In R, the qnorm() function takes a probability and tells you the exact value where the area under the standard normal distribution curve reaches that amount.
E.g., 40% of the distribution falls to the left of:

qnorm(0.4)

[1] -0.253


And 50% of the distribution falls to the left of…
(we actually don’t need to calculate this - take a look above at the plot and think!)

qnorm(0.5)

[1] 0





In a “standard normal” distribution – a normal distribution with mean of 0 and sd of 1, often written “N(0,1)” – 90% of the distribution falls below 1.28. In other words, there is a 90% probability that a randomly drawn observation is < 1.28.
Given this information, if we make the assumption for now that outlook is normally distributed, we should be able to figure out the value of the original outlook variable at which we would expect 90% of the distribution to fall.
As we calculated the Z scores using \(Z = \frac{x - M}{SD}\), we are essentially asking what value of \(X\) results in \(Z = 1.28\).
We’ll take this opportunity ot introduce an alternative way to access variables in a dataframe. As well as calculating means and standard deviations using data |> summarise(), we can also get a specific variable using data$variable. This is easier for doing quick calculations such as:
The Z score for some hypothetical person who scored 20 on the optimism question:

(20 - mean(sdata$outlook)) / sd(sdata$outlook)

[1] 0.106


Task: can you rearrange \(1.28 = \frac{x - M}{SD}\), and then figure out the value at which 90% of outlook scores are below?





Solution



Solution 4. 

(1.28*sd(sdata$outlook)) + mean(sdata$outlook)

[1] 69.9






Question 5


Find the outlook value for one of your group members. They will need to remember the pseudonym used to fill the survey.
We can extract a specific row with the filter() function, where we use two equals signs to ask “is a variable equal to <specific value>?”.
For example, to find any row where the pseudonym “dougal” was used:

sdata |> 
  filter(pseudonym == "dougal")

Assuming outlook is normally distributed, what is the probability of seeing somebody less optimistic than your chosen group member? And more optimistic?
Do the values satisfy the requirements of probabilities? Check that they are positive, less than 1, and they sum to 1

TODO flashcard pnorm? or link to lectures?






Solution



Solution 5. Dougal is a little bit of a pessimist:

sdata |> 
  filter(pseudonym == "dougal") |>
  select(pseudonym, outlook)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  pseudonym outlook
  <chr>       <dbl>
1 dougal        -16


His outlook score of 16, when transformed to a Z-score, is:

dougalZ = (-16 - mean(sdata$outlook)) / sd(sdata$outlook)

There is a 23% probability of seeing someone less optimistic than Dougal, and a 77% probability of seeing someone more optimistic.

pnorm(dougalZ)

[1] 0.229

1-pnorm(dougalZ)

[1] 0.771
